newsitem.title: INDIA: India says wins $6.7 billion in official aid.
newsitem.headline: India says wins $6.7 billion in official aid.

text.p: India said that international donors meeting in Paris on Wednesday pledged some $6.7 billion in aid, about the same as last year's $6.6 billion, in a show of support for the nation's economic reforms.

The government said in a statement released in New Delhi: "India's economic reforms received strong support and endorsement from the community of bilateral and multilateral donors assembled in Paris."

The annual India Development Forum meetings on Tuesday and Wednesday in Paris were held under the aegis of the World Bank and attended by representatives of the Asian Development Bank, the European Commission and International Monetary Fund (IMF).

The $6.7 billion pledge was in line with the expectations of Indian officials, who said the country had stepped up utilisation of external assistance in the 1996/97 fiscal year which ended on March 31.
The new aid package, supported by governments and multilateral organisations, is for the current 1997/98 fiscal year.

"Many delegations expressed appreciation of India's performance since 1991 and complimented the Gujral government for continuing the reform process despite the difficulties of managing a coalition," the statement said.
Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's 15-party centre-left coalition has pressed ahead with free-market reforms which were initiated in 1991 when India faced a balance of payments crisis.

Finance Secretary Montek Singh Ahluwalia, who headed the Indian delegation to the Paris talks, said the government would soon announce decisions stemming from a review of anti-poverty programmes, the statement said.
Earlier this year, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram said the programmes needed to be reduced in number and better focused.

Ahluwalia said India shared the World Bank's "anxiety" over the need for sustained and rapid economic growth to combat poverty, and said there was good reason to believe that the recent acceleration in growth had reduced poverty.

The finance secretary said India will need some $400 billion in investments over the next decade to pay for infrastructure, and the bulk of the financing in the short term will have to be made by the public sector.
A slowdown in export growth in 1996/97 was exaggerated by the appreciation of the U.S. dollar, and the current account deficit was 1.2 percent of gross domestic product, he said.
Foreign investment, both direct and portfolio, totalled $6.4 billion in 1996/97, helping to add $5.3 billion to foreign exchange reserves, he said.
"The increase in private capital flows is a very positive development which demonstrates continued investor confidence in the Indian economy," the statement said.
Ahluwalia said a recent slowdown in industrial growth was partly due to declining world trade.

The Finance Ministry official appealed for more aid "in view of the progress made in the past six years which has brought the economy to a point where more and more people both inside India and outside see the implementation potential of the Indian economy".

The statement quoted IMF senior adviser David Goldsbrough as congratulating India for "managing a complex fiscal situation while emphasising the need for further reduction of the overall public sector deficit".
